name: Question 11
problem:
A meteorologist measured two particular features, ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ at various locations throughout California. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular location. 
The first and second principal components of the data are approximately

$$
{v}_{1}≈[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.745\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}≈[\begin{aligned}-0.745 \\ 0.667\end{aligned}].
$$

By combining the two measured features linearly, the meteorologist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?
worked_solution:
Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the *first principal component* of the data.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14198769/assets/f7c823606bbbe77326819df5d487b5e0019dd7439b46124547f71681b9484f6d.png)

 

Let  

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0.667 & -0.745 \\ 0.745 & 0.667\end{aligned}]
$$

be the matrix of principal components. 

Then, applying the change of variables $Y=XV,$ we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are uncorrelated), and

- the features ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in ${y}_{1}$).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]V \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0.667 & -0.745 \\ 0.745 & 0.667\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2} & -0.745{x}_{1}+0.667{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we have that ${y}_{1}=0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2}$ will contain most of the variance of the data. 

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

$$
{y}_{1}=0.667{x}_{1}+0.745{x}_{2}.
$$

html:
Question 11
?

A meteorologist measured two particular features, x1 and x2, at various locations throughout California. The collected data was stored in a standardized observation matrix, where each row contains both features for a particular location. The first and second principal components of the data are approximately v1≈[0.6670.745],v2≈[−0.7450.667].

By combining the two measured features linearly, the meteorologist wants to construct a single feature that preserves the maximum amount of variance of the collected data. Which of the following could be the best candidate for the new feature?

a
 −0.745x1+0.667x2
b
0.667x1+0.745x2
c
 0.667x1−0.745x2
d
0.667(x1+x2)
e
0.745x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the direction in which the data varies the most (the direction where we have the maximum variance) corresponds to the first principal component of the data.

Let

V=[||v1v2||]=[0.667−0.7450.7450.667]

be the matrix of principal components.

Then, applying the change of variables Y=XV, we can convert our observation matrix X into a new matrix Y of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of Y is diagonal (meaning that the new features y1 and y2 are uncorrelated), and

  • the features y1 and y2 are arranged in order of decreasing variance (meaning that most of the variance is concentrated in y1).

Applying our change of variables to a single observation x=[x1x2], we get

[y1y2]=[x1x2]V=[x1x2][0.667−0.7450.7450.667]=[0.667x1+0.745x2−0.745x1+0.667x2].

As a result, we have that y1=0.667x1+0.745x2 will contain most of the variance of the data.

Therefore, the best candidate for the new single feature is

y1=0.667x1+0.745x2.
